cover.title: National Nuclear Physics Initiative
cover.subtitle: A Community Action Framework for Realizing the Mega Science Vision–2035
cover.message: INPA invites comments on this proposed framework before its finalisation through community consultation. The draft sets out ways to connect scientific priorities with collaborative programmes, institutional responsibility and opportunities for young researchers.

response.text: Please send comments and suggestions to
, with a copy to Prof. Ashok Kumar Jain at
. Please identify the relevant section when suggesting a change.

blocks.text: Nuclear physics stands at the threshold of a transformative era. Rapid advances in accelerator technology, detector systems, radioactive ion beams, high-performance computing, artificial intelligence, and theoretical modelling are opening unprecedented opportunities to explore the fundamental properties of atomic nuclei and their interactions. These advances are not only deepening our understanding of the strong interaction and the origin of the elements, but are also driving innovations in energy, healthcare, materials science, national security, and space science.

India has made significant contributions to this global scientific enterprise through sustained investments in research infrastructure, national laboratories, universities, and international collaborations. Over the past several decades, Indian scientists have built internationally recognized programmes in nuclear structure, nuclear reactions, nuclear astrophysics, accelerator science, detector development, nuclear theory, and applications. This strong foundation provides an exceptional opportunity to shape the next phase of national growth in nuclear science.

text.text: Recognizing this opportunity, the Indian nuclear physics community prepared the
Mega Science Vision–2035: Nuclear Physics

, a comprehensive document that articulates the scientific aspirations, infrastructure priorities, and strategic recommendations required for maintaining India's leadership in nuclear physics during the coming decade. The Vision document identifies major scientific challenges, recommends new facilities and technologies, emphasizes the importance of detector development, nuclear theory, advanced computing, human resource development, and international partnerships, and presents a national roadmap for the future of the discipline.
The publication of the
Mega Science Vision–2035
represents an important milestone for Indian nuclear physics. However, every national vision naturally raises a second question:

blocks.text: How can the scientific community collectively transform this vision into sustained national action?

text.text: It is this question that motivates the
National Nuclear Physics Initiative (NNPI)
The NNPI is not another vision document. Rather, it is a community-driven action framework designed to translate the recommendations of the
Mega Science Vision–2035

into coordinated national programmes. It seeks to connect researchers, universities, national laboratories, accelerator facilities, industries, funding agencies, and international partners through a shared commitment to scientific excellence, collaboration, innovation, and human resource development.

blocks.text: The Initiative is founded on a simple but powerful conviction:
Scientific excellence flourishes when people, institutions, ideas, and infrastructure are connected through a common national purpose.

text.text: This philosophy is embodied in the guiding motto of the Initiative:
Connecting People and Enabling Discovery

This motto reflects the belief that discovery is not the product of individual laboratories alone, but of a vibrant scientific ecosystem in which experimentalists, theorists, instrumentation scientists, computational physicists, engineers, students, educators, and policy makers work together to address common scientific challenges.

blocks.text: Accordingly, the NNPI complements the Mega Science Vision–2035 in a distinctive way. While the Vision document defines what India seeks to achieve, the NNPI focuses on how the nuclear physics community can organize itself to achieve these aspirations through coordinated national action. It therefore places particular emphasis on strengthening scientific networks, integrating experiment with theory and computation, developing advanced instrumentation, nurturing future generations of researchers, promoting national and international collaboration, and creating sustainable mechanisms for community participation.

The Indian Nuclear Physics Association (INPA) provides the natural community platform for this endeavour. As the national professional association representing the nuclear physics community, INPA is uniquely positioned to foster dialogue, encourage collaboration, facilitate dissemination of knowledge, support young researchers, and serve as a catalyst for implementing many of the community-oriented recommendations envisioned in this framework.

text.text: This document is therefore intended as a community action framework. It proposes practical pathways through which the Indian nuclear physics community can work collectively to realize the aspirations articulated in the Mega Science Vision–2035. By integrating scientific excellence with institutional cooperation, human resource development, digital connectivity, and sustained national engagement, the
NNPI
seeks to strengthen India's nuclear physics ecosystem and enhance its contribution to science, technology, and society in the decades ahead.

blocks.text: The NNPI translates the aspirations of the Mega Science Vision–2035 into coordinated national action by strengthening scientific pillars, fostering collaboration, developing human resources, and building an integrated research ecosystem. The Indian Nuclear Physics Association (INPA) provides the community platform that connects people and enables discovery.

sections.title: 1.2 Why a National Nuclear Physics Initiative?

blocks.text: The Mega Science Vision–2035 sets out the scientific questions and capabilities India should pursue. NNPI gives the nuclear physics community a way to turn those priorities into programmes that institutions can lead and the relevant agencies can evaluate.

Modern nuclear physics draws on capabilities spread across national laboratories, universities and research institutes. A sustained community planning process can bring those strengths together around a scientific question, identify what is missing and form collaborations that can carry the work forward. INPA can convene that process, while participating institutions retain responsibility for their programmes.

Experiment, theory, instrumentation, computation and nuclear data need to develop together. Better coordination can make existing facilities easier to use, show where upgrades would make a difference and guide investment in capabilities India will need. International collaborations can extend scientific reach and help develop expertise that can be used at home.

The initiative also needs to create opportunities for the people who will sustain these programmes. Alongside training and access to facilities, early-career researchers need scope to propose and lead work of their own. Instrumentation, analysis software and practical training can also offer routes into entrepreneurship where institutions have a clear need.

blocks.alt: Flowchart showing how new scientific questions lead to priorities, capabilities, experiments, interpretation and further questions.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.2. Science-Led Planning of Nuclear Physics: From Scientific Questions to Capabilities and Discovery.

blocks.text: Chapter 2 sets out the capabilities and partnerships that NNPI should develop. Chapter 3 explains how priorities can become programmes with institutional ownership, appropriate support and independent review.

chapters.label: National Nuclear Physics Initiative  /  Chapter 2
chapters.title: Building the National Nuclear Physics Ecosystem

blocks.text: The scientific questions identified through the planning process in Chapter 1 should determine what NNPI undertakes. Each proposed programme should explain the question it will address, how the work will be carried out, which groups should take part and what capabilities they will need.

Programmes can begin with a calculation, a detector prototype or a few measurements at an existing accelerator. A collaboration can expand once early results justify the effort and participating institutions are ready to commit. Chapter 3 describes how programmes of different scales can be developed and reviewed.
Bringing existing expertise together

A scientific network can connect experimentalists, theorists, instrumentation teams, computational specialists and nuclear-data experts around a common problem. It can give groups at smaller institutions access to equipment, data and expertise while giving them a voice in setting the scientific agenda. A network should have enough organisation to share work and facilities effectively. Its structure should grow with the scale of the programme.

Universities should be able to originate and lead programmes. NNPI can strengthen active groups, help rebuild declining ones and support new groups through faculty visits, joint supervision and access to national facilities. Where nuclear physics has a limited presence, including at some IISERs, modern courses and early research experience can help establish a foothold.

A mature proposal should identify the scientific outcomes, the participating institutions, the equipment and people needed, and the first milestones. A small collaboration may need only a convincing science case and arrangements for access. A programme that calls for substantial investment will also need firm institutional commitments and a credible plan for review. Exploratory support gives teams a chance to build that case through actual work.

The national portfolio should be reviewed periodically. New ideas can enter at modest scale, successful collaborations can grow and programmes that have achieved their purpose can conclude. Young researchers should have opportunities to propose work and lead these collaborations from the outset.

India’s experimental capabilities should be developed as a network of complementary facilities. Host institutions can retain their scientific identities while coordinating access, planned upgrades and experimental campaigns. An INPA/NNPI facilities directory, maintained with the hosts, could show available beams, energies and intensities, instruments, access procedures and contacts.
Access from proposal to analysis

Facilities built with public investment should provide transparent scientific access to external users. An allocation of beam time is only one part of that access. A university team may also need targets, detectors, electronics, travel support, help with data acquisition and time to analyse the results. Facility plans should account for these needs, especially when a young investigator is leading an experiment for the first time.

A facility directory should make clear which instruments are installed, which are shared and which need to be brought by the user. Host laboratories and university groups could use this information to plan complementary experiments and coordinate requests for scarce beam time. The arrangements should be developed with facility managers and users.

Scientific reviews of facilities should consider reliability and beam availability alongside the originality of the research, the range of users, new techniques and collaborations, and the opportunities given to students and early-career scientists. Universities can contribute targets, detectors, analysis software and experimental methods of their own.
Renewing facilities and creating new capabilities

Before proposing a new facility, the community should establish which measurements are needed and whether better scheduling, improved instruments or an accelerator upgrade could make them possible. A proposal for major investment should compare domestic construction, upgrades, shared access and international participation. Vision–2035 identifies capabilities such as high-current stable beams, radioactive-ion beams and specialised underground facilities as areas for long-term planning.

Modernisation can include improved ion sources, beam quality and intensity, target preparation, separators, electronics or data acquisition. Each investment should be tied to a specific gain in measurement capability. A new facility becomes easier to justify once the community can show which capability it needs and what the alternatives would deliver.

Participation in international facilities such as FAIR can give Indian teams access to capabilities that are difficult to reproduce domestically. Technology and expertise developed through these collaborations should feed back into Indian research and training. A practical test of the national system is whether an early-career researcher with a strong idea can gain the support needed to lead an experiment.

Better detectors and electronics can open measurements that were previously out of reach. Instrumentation should therefore have its own scientific programme, with priorities drawn from the experiments and capabilities the community wants to develop. India should strengthen its ability to design, integrate, test, repair and improve important systems, drawing on domestic and international suppliers where appropriate.

blocks.caption: Figure 2.1. Conceptual illustration of detector and electronics testing before an accelerator experiment. AI-generated image.

blocks.text: A network for building and sharing instruments

text.text: The National Detector Development and Training Centre proposed in Vision–2035 [1, Section 5.4, pp. 97–98] could provide shared facilities for specialised fabrication, precision machining, detector characterisation and electronics testing. Universities and smaller laboratories could develop components such as silicon detectors, targets, front-end electronics, digital data-acquisition modules and simulation tools. Competitive prototype grants would give young investigators a manageable project to lead and room to test and revise their designs.

blocks.text: University projects could start with a prototype small enough for a student or postdoctoral researcher to help design, assemble and test. Successful designs can then be integrated into an experiment or developed into a system for several users. Early tests should establish performance, identify faults and show what needs to change before the next round of development.

text.text: Where practical, detector arrays and specialised electronics could be shared across accelerators. This requires clear access arrangements and support for transport, installation, operation and maintenance. A networked
National Nuclear Instrumentation Programme

could coordinate these activities and connect laboratories with industry. Laboratories would define the scientific requirements and test prototypes. Industry partners would help make reliable, reproducible equipment that can be manufactured and supported.

blocks.text: Industry partnerships could focus on capabilities needed at several laboratories, such as vacuum systems, precision components, fast electronics and digital signal processing. A laboratory can provide a demanding test environment, while an industrial partner can assess production and long-term support. Priorities should be identified from the scientific programme and the needs that facilities have in common.
Passing on practical expertise

text.text: Critical skills often reside with the people who build and operate instruments. Laboratories should identify these skills well before senior staff retire and provide time for them to work alongside younger colleagues. Documentation should cover assembly, commissioning, troubleshooting and maintenance. Longer hands-on attachments at detector centres and laboratories would give students, researchers and technical staff opportunities to learn these methods through practice.

blocks.text: An instrumentation programme should periodically identify who holds critical expertise, who is learning it and whether there is enough overlap for the younger team to take over. Retired experts can help where their experience is still needed. Younger teams should have opportunities to improve the methods they inherit.

Theory should help shape experiments from the proposal stage. A calculation can identify a measurement that distinguishes between competing models, and an unexpected result can prompt a new calculation or a different experiment. Larger programmes should involve experimentalists, theorists, computational specialists and nuclear-data evaluators early enough to influence the research design.
A national centre and a distributed theory network

text.text: Sustained positions in nuclear theory are limited. NNPI should examine a small, permanent
National Centre for Nuclear Theory

with a core research group, computing resources, postdoctoral positions and visiting appointments. It could anchor a distributed network linking universities, IITs, institutes and national laboratories. Competitive fellowships hosted by participating institutions could help young theorists establish independent programmes and build groups where nuclear physics is thinly represented.

blocks.text: Theory and computation can also help introduce nuclear physics to institutions without a large experimental facility. Visiting appointments, access to computing and close contact with experimental groups can give those teams a research base and help them take part in national programmes.
Computing, software and evaluated data

text.text: NNPI

should improve access to high-performance computing and support the people who develop and maintain scientific codes. Useful codes should have documentation, validation cases and an arrangement for long-term maintenance. Artificial intelligence and machine learning can help with pattern recognition, uncertainty analysis and faster models. Their outputs should be checked against physical constraints, calculations and measurements.

blocks.text: Computing support includes suitable software, well-tested algorithms and access to specialist advice. For codes used across institutions, a group should be responsible for maintaining releases and passing on expertise as researchers move on. Shared validation cases can help users reproduce results and understand where a calculation can be trusted.

Nuclear data work brings together measurement, modelling, evaluation and uncertainty assessment. Reliable masses, half-lives, decay schemes, cross sections and fission yields serve basic research, astrophysics, reactor studies and medical applications. NNPI can help users and researchers identify priority data gaps and organise joint measurement and evaluation programmes. These projects can offer young scientists well-defined work that uses existing facilities.

sections.title: 2.5 The Next Generation: Empowering Young Researchers

text.text: Students need early exposure to contemporary nuclear physics, from exotic nuclei and astrophysics to detectors, computation and applications.

Modern courses, summer schools, internships and research attachments could extend that exposure, particularly at campuses where the subject has a limited presence. Joint supervision can connect students at smaller institutions with working research groups and national facilities.

blocks.text: A student interested in experiments might spend a term at an accelerator laboratory or work with a detector-development group. A young theorist could spend time with an experimental team to learn how measurements and their uncertainties are obtained. Similar attachments with industry could give instrumentation researchers experience of fabrication and testing.

blocks.alt: Conceptual illustration of early-career researchers demonstrating a laboratory prototype.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.2. Conceptual illustration of early-career researchers demonstrating a laboratory prototype. AI-generated image.

blocks.text: From training to independent work

Support is especially important when researchers move from postdoctoral work into independent careers. Modest seed grants, exploratory beam time, prototype support and theory or computational fellowships can give young researchers a project of their own. A carefully designed exploratory study can be valuable even when it rules out an approach. Attachments should be long enough for participants to contribute and bring skills back to their home institutions.

Mentorship should give younger colleagues increasing responsibility for proposals, experiments, instruments and collaborations. Early- and mid-career researchers should also be represented in INPA working groups and community planning, with scope to propose new directions and question established priorities.

A sustained career path should connect student projects and doctoral training with postdoctoral work, independent projects and leadership. The theory centre and fellowships proposed in Section 2.4 could improve continuity for young theorists. Experimentalists, instrumentation specialists, computational physicists and nuclear-data researchers need comparable opportunities to establish their own work.
Entrepreneurship as an additional career pathway

The limited availability of conventional research positions makes it important to create additional career pathways for young nuclear scientists. NNPI should help interested researchers turn their skills in instrumentation, software, data analysis and training into products and services that institutions need. INPA can identify problems with prospective users, connect young teams with laboratories and incubators, and help arrange trials. The first initiatives should be small enough for a young team to deliver and support, with a clear route to a paying customer and evidence of demand beyond the first host institution.

The proposed collaboration among INPA, IIT Ropar and Ushankk Nuclear Academy illustrates how training partnerships could open a route to entrepreneurship. Young researchers could be invited to develop teaching modules, analysis software or laboratory exercises in response to needs identified by instructors and industry practitioners. A training programme could provide a first setting in which to test the material and improve it. A team could then assess whether other institutions would pay for the product or service and whether that income would cover the cost of keeping it up to date and supporting users.
Every major NNPI initiative should be able to show how it helps younger researchers move from learning and contributing to taking responsibility and leading work of their own.

sections.title: 3.1 From Scientific Priority to an Executable Programme

blocks.text: The community-planning process described in Chapter 1 identifies important scientific directions, while Chapter 2 establishes the ecosystem of people, facilities, instrumentation, theory, computation and partnerships required to pursue them. The next challenge is to convert these priorities into programmes capable of implementation.

This transition is critical. A scientifically compelling idea does not become executable merely because the community agrees that it is important. It must acquire sufficient definition for institutions to assume responsibility, funding agencies to evaluate it, resources to be committed, and progress to be assessed.
NNPI should therefore provide a pathway through which a scientific priority can progressively mature into an implementable programme.
The process begins with defining a programme. It also requires institutional ownership, resources for implementation and scientific review.
Programme definition

text.text: Once an emerging priority has acquired sufficient scientific support, an appropriate
NNPI Working Group
should help develop it into a
Programme Definition Document

blocks.text: This should not initially be an elaborate project report. Its purpose is to answer a limited set of essential questions: What is the scientific objective? Why is it important now? What capability is required? What already exists in India? Who could participate and lead? What approximate resources and timescale are involved? What would constitute scientific success?

For larger programmes, this initial document could subsequently develop into a detailed project proposal through the participating institutions. The important point is that the scientific programme should be defined before the administrative machinery surrounding it becomes dominant.
Different programmes require different pathways

NNPI will deal with activities spanning very different scales—from exploratory projects proposed by young investigators to major national facilities. It would therefore be counterproductive to subject all programmes to identical procedures.

An exploratory theoretical idea or detector prototype might require modest resources and rapid scientific evaluation. A collaborative experimental programme might require coordinated access to existing facilities. A national detector-development programme could require sustained multi-institutional support. A new accelerator facility would require extensive technical studies, governmental approval and long-term investment.

text.text: Planning and review must be rigorous, but proportional to the scale, cost and complexity of the programme.

blocks.text: This is particularly important for small science and young researchers. A system designed primarily around mega-projects can inadvertently make modest innovative projects disproportionately difficult to initiate.
Scientific maturity before institutional commitment

Not every promising idea should immediately become a national programme. NNPI should allow ideas to mature through workshops, working groups, exploratory calculations, proof-of-concept experiments and small collaborative projects. This permits the scientific case to strengthen—or, equally importantly, allows weaknesses to become apparent—before substantial resources are committed.
This also allows genuinely new ideas to compete on scientific merit without requiring their proponents to possess large institutional structures from the beginning.
From Vision–2035 to an organised nuclear physics community

text.text: The Mega Science Vision–2035 did not envisage publication of the Vision document as the end of the planning process. In his message accompanying the report, dated 14 September 2023, Prof. Ajay K. Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, wrote [1]:
“I wish the Indian nuclear physics community all the best for organizing themselves and taking the next required steps to turn the vision outlined in this Report into a reality.”

blocks.text: The Vision document itself further recommended the creation of an Indian Nuclear Science Society [1, Section 5.2(f), p. 96]. An Indian Nuclear Society already existed with its own established identity and constituency. In taking forward the broader intent of the Vision document, the nuclear physics community therefore constituted the Indian Nuclear Physics Association (INPA), giving the new organisation a distinct identity and an explicit focus on nuclear physics.

text.text: The establishment of INPA can thus be viewed as a practical response to the larger objective articulated in Vision–2035: to enable the nuclear physics community to organise itself and take the next required steps towards translating the Vision into reality.
NNPI

represents the next stage of this process. It seeks to provide the continuing community mechanism through which scientific priorities can be identified, programmes developed, institutions connected and constructive dialogue established with the agencies whose support is ultimately required for implementation.
INPA provides continuity to the community process; it does not replace the responsibilities of institutions or funding agencies.

blocks.text: Identifying ownership

Once a programme has matured sufficiently, responsibility must become clear. INPA can facilitate community discussion, establish working groups and help develop the scientific case, but INPA should not ordinarily become the implementing institution.
Instead, an appropriate university, laboratory, institute or consortium should assume ownership of the programme and develop the formal proposal required by the relevant funding agency.

text.text:
INPA / NNPI — Scientific priority, community consultation and facilitation
Institution / Consortium — Programme ownership and implementation
Funding Agency — Independent evaluation, funding and oversight

blocks.text: This separation protects both scientific independence and institutional responsibility.
From community priority to agency consideration

An NNPI programme emerging from a transparent community process should carry a significance beyond that of an isolated institutional proposal. It indicates that the scientific case has been considered in the context of the broader development of nuclear physics in India.
But NNPI endorsement should not replace independent peer review by a funding agency.

text.text: Community endorsement establishes strategic relevance; agency evaluation establishes fundability.

blocks.text: The two functions are complementary. This is also where INPA must progressively develop constructive relationships with DAE, DST, ANRF and other relevant agencies. Such relationships should arise through consultation and demonstrated usefulness rather than through claims of administrative authority.
Developing recognition through credibility
INPA's role as an interface between the nuclear-physics community and funding agencies cannot simply be declared. It must be earned.
Credibility grows through broad representation, transparent planning, useful recommendations and dialogue with agencies.

Initially, this may involve inviting appropriate representatives of funding and implementing agencies to selected NNPI consultations, sharing emerging programme priorities with them, and understanding existing funding mechanisms before proposals reach an advanced stage.
Over time, if NNPI consistently produces scientifically strong, realistic and community-supported programmes, its recommendations should naturally acquire greater weight.
The objective is therefore recognition through usefulness rather than authority through designation.
Maintaining dialogue during programme development

Interaction with agencies should not begin only when a completed proposal arrives seeking funds. For major programmes, early dialogue can identify practical constraints, possible funding routes, opportunities for inter-agency cooperation and requirements that should be considered during programme development.

This does not mean that funding agencies should determine scientific priorities. Nor should INPA determine agency decisions. It means creating a constructive interface between scientific aspiration and implementation reality.

Eventually, this interaction could evolve into a periodic Nuclear Physics Community–Agency Forum, bringing together INPA, relevant agencies, major institutions and programme leaders to discuss emerging priorities, programmes approaching implementation, bottlenecks and new opportunities.
Such a forum need not become another permanent administrative structure. Its value would lie in maintaining dialogue.
The guiding principle

The institutional architecture of NNPI should remain deliberately light. INPA should neither become a funding agency nor seek operational control over programmes implemented by universities and laboratories. Its strength should derive from representing the scientific community, sustaining long-term planning and helping good scientific ideas find viable pathways toward implementation.

text.text: NNPI should acquire influence through scientific credibility, community legitimacy and demonstrated usefulness—not through administrative authority.

blocks.text: A scientific programme begins with an idea, but it becomes implementable only when individuals and institutions are prepared to take responsibility for carrying it forward. Community endorsement establishes scientific relevance; resources make implementation possible; but neither can substitute for clear scientific leadership and institutional ownership.

Many NNPI programmes will be collaborative and may involve universities, national laboratories, accelerator centres, theory groups, technology partners and, in some cases, industry. Their collaborative character must be preserved. At the same time, responsibility cannot become so widely distributed that no one is ultimately accountable for progress.

text.text: Collective vision requires identifiable responsibility.

blocks.text: Scientific leadership should emerge with the programme

Scientific leadership should arise naturally during the process through which an emerging idea develops into a programme. The person who first proposes an idea need not necessarily become the eventual programme leader. As the programme develops, additional expertise may enter, the scientific objectives may broaden, and a group of researchers may emerge who are best placed to carry it forward.

NNPI should facilitate this process rather than appoint leadership prematurely. By the time substantial institutional commitments or resources are sought, however, the programme should have clearly identifiable scientific leadership capable of articulating its objectives, bringing together the required expertise and maintaining scientific direction during implementation.
Scientific leadership and project administration are different

Scientific leadership and project administration are both necessary, particularly for large programmes, but they should not be confused. Scientific leadership must continually ask whether the programme is addressing the right scientific questions, whether the methods remain appropriate, whether new developments have changed the scientific landscape, whether the required capabilities are being created, and whether younger researchers are acquiring meaningful responsibility. Project administration addresses expenditure, procurement, personnel, schedules, reporting and institutional procedures.

text.text: Scientific leadership protects the purpose of the programme; project management enables its execution.

blocks.text: For small programmes these responsibilities may reside with the same person. As scale increases, appropriate administrative and technical support should accompany scientific leadership.
Institutional ownership

Once a programme reaches the stage of formal implementation, an appropriate institution or consortium of institutions must assume responsibility. INPA/NNPI can help identify the scientific priority, develop the programme, connect potential collaborators and facilitate dialogue with agencies. But it should not normally become the implementing body.

text.text:
INPA / NNPI — Community process and scientific facilitation
Institution / Consortium — Ownership and implementation
Funding Agency — Evaluation, resources and oversight

blocks.text: For some programmes, the natural institutional home will be obvious. An accelerator upgrade, for example, will normally be anchored at the facility concerned. For a distributed instrumentation programme, nuclear-data initiative or collaborative scientific network, however, a consortium model may be more appropriate.
Ownership should follow capability and commitment

The lead institution should not automatically be the largest or most established institution, nor should ownership necessarily belong to the institution from which the original idea emerged. The appropriate home should be determined by scientific capability, relevant infrastructure, commitment to the programme, ability to provide continuity, collaborative culture, opportunities for younger researchers, and capacity to fulfil the proposed responsibility.

text.text: National programmes should strengthen the national ecosystem, not merely the institution that hosts them.

blocks.text: A national programme located at one institution should therefore create opportunities and capabilities extending beyond its institutional boundary.
Meaningful consortia

For many programmes, a consortium will be the natural implementation mechanism. But a long list of participating institutions does not necessarily constitute a genuine collaboration. Each major partner should have a clearly identifiable scientific, technological or implementation responsibility.

text.text: If a participating institution were removed, what capability or responsibility would the programme lose?

blocks.text: If the answer is essentially none, its participation may be nominal rather than substantive. A consortium should therefore be constructed around complementarity of capabilities, not merely breadth of representation.
Responsibility must be matched by authority and resources

It is ineffective to assign responsibility to an individual or institution without providing sufficient authority to make necessary decisions or the resources required to carry them out. Equally, substantial resources cannot be provided without corresponding responsibility and accountability.

text.text: Responsibility should be supported by authority and resources, with clear accountability.

blocks.text: The balance should apply at every level—from a national programme to a university group responsible for one detector subsystem, theoretical calculation or data activity.
Leadership succession must begin early

Many nuclear-physics programmes, particularly those involving major facilities or technology development, extend over periods comparable with a substantial fraction of a scientist's career. A programme whose continuity depends upon one or two senior individuals therefore contains an inherent vulnerability. Leadership succession should consequently not begin when a programme leader approaches retirement.

Young and mid-career researchers should progressively be entrusted with responsibility for scientific work packages, experiments, instrumentation systems, theoretical programmes and collaborative groups.

This is more than manpower planning. It transfers scientific judgement, accumulated experience and institutional memory. The treasure of knowledge residing with experienced scientists and technical personnel, discussed in Section 2.3, can be preserved only when the next generation works alongside them sufficiently long to acquire both explicit knowledge and the tacit understanding that cannot easily be written into manuals.
Young researchers must receive real responsibility

It is relatively easy to include young scientists in national programmes. It is more difficult—and much more important—to give them intellectual ownership. NNPI programmes should therefore deliberately create identifiable components that younger researchers can lead, such as an experiment, detector subsystem, computational development, theoretical problem, nuclear-data activity or emerging scientific direction.

The purpose is not to create artificial leadership positions. Responsibility must be earned through capability. But once capability is demonstrated, seniority alone should not determine scientific authority.
Continuity without permanent ownership

Institutions may provide continuity, but scientific leadership should not become permanent ownership by individuals or groups. A successful national programme should be capable of absorbing new people and new ideas and, eventually, of changing leadership. Otherwise programmes can gradually become identified with particular individuals rather than with their scientific objectives.

text.text: People build programmes; programmes build communities; communities should outlive their founders.

blocks.text: INPA's role after implementation begins

Once a programme receives funding and enters implementation, INPA's role should change—but not disappear. INPA should not supervise expenditure, procurement or institutional administration. Those responsibilities belong to the implementing institutions and funding agencies.

But NNPI is intended to be a continuous community-planning process. INPA should therefore remain informed about the broad scientific progress of programmes that have emerged through NNPI. The purpose is not oversight; it is community learning: what worked, what difficulties arose, what capabilities were created, which young groups emerged, what new scientific questions appeared, and whether barriers recur across several programmes.
This feedback loop prevents NNPI from becoming a sequence of planning documents disconnected from implementation.
A light governance principle

For larger collaborative programmes, some form of scientific leadership group will clearly be required. NNPI should not prescribe its detailed composition or rules at this stage; different programmes will require different arrangements.

text.text: Governance should be sufficient to establish responsibility and continuity, but no more elaborate than the scale of the programme requires.

sections.title: 3.3 A Tiered Pathway from Ideas to National Programmes

blocks.text: Scientific ideas emerge at very different levels of maturity and require very different scales of support. Some may initially need only a small exploratory calculation, measurement or prototype. Others may already involve established collaborations and substantial infrastructure. A few may ultimately justify creation of a major national capability or participation in a mega-science initiative.

NNPI should therefore provide a tiered but flexible pathway through which promising scientific ideas can receive support appropriate to their stage of development. The objective is to allow ideas to start at an appropriate scale, demonstrate scientific value, attract the necessary expertise and progressively acquire larger commitments when justified.

text.text: Every major programme begins as an idea; not every good idea needs to begin as a major programme.

blocks.text: Tier I — Exploratory Initiatives

The first tier should provide space for new ideas, scientific risk and proof of concept. These may include exploratory experiments, theoretical investigations, detector or electronics prototypes, computational developments, nuclear-data studies, new analytical techniques or interdisciplinary applications.

Such initiatives will normally require modest resources and should be capable of relatively rapid evaluation. They are particularly important for young investigators, for whom a small independent project may provide the first opportunity to establish scientific ownership.
The principal question at this stage is: Is the idea sufficiently promising to explore further?
A successful Tier I project need not necessarily become larger. It may answer an important question at modest scale and conclude successfully.
Tier II — Collaborative Scientific Programmes

Some ideas will require a broader range of expertise, coordinated experiments or access to capabilities distributed across institutions. A single investigator’s idea can then become a shared scientific programme.

Tier II programmes would normally involve several research groups or institutions working around a clearly defined scientific objective, often making coordinated use of existing facilities and infrastructure. They could include experimental campaigns, theory–experiment collaborations, detector or instrumentation projects, coordinated nuclear-data activities and emerging interdisciplinary programmes.
INPA/NNPI can play an important role at this stage by bringing together interested groups, identifying complementary expertise and helping an effective scientific collaboration to emerge.
Tier III — National Capability Programmes

Some scientific objectives require more than collaboration around existing resources. They require creation or substantial strengthening of a capability that can serve a wider community over an extended period.

Such programmes could involve major instrumentation systems, specialised beam capabilities, detector-development infrastructure, sustained nuclear-data programmes, advanced computational resources or national centres and networks such as the proposed National Centre for Nuclear Theory.
The central test at this level is: Will this programme create a capability that enables a wider community to undertake science that would otherwise not be possible?

Tier III initiatives will normally require stronger institutional ownership, sustained funding and formal mechanisms for national access and participation. Their value should be judged not only by the science produced by the host institution, but by the new scientific capability created for the national community.
Tier IV — Major National and Mega-Science Initiatives

A smaller number of scientific programmes may eventually justify major national infrastructure or substantial participation in international mega-science projects. These initiatives require strong scientific justification, broad community engagement, substantial technical preparation, long-term financial commitment and appropriate governmental approval.

Vision–2035 recognises the special demands of such projects and envisages community planning and early consultation mechanisms for major new initiatives [1, Sections 5.1–5.2, pp. 92–96]. NNPI should build upon rather than duplicate these mechanisms.
Choosing a tier that fits the programme
The tiers describe increasing scale and commitment—not a compulsory sequence.

A programme need not mechanically pass through every tier. A mature scientific community responding to an important international opportunity may legitimately begin at Tier III or Tier IV. Conversely, an excellent research programme may remain at Tier I or Tier II throughout its lifetime and produce outstanding science.
Progression must depend upon evidence

Movement toward a larger commitment should never be automatic. At appropriate stages, the programme should ask whether the scientific case has strengthened; whether the concept or required technology has been demonstrated; whether an effective scientific community has emerged around it; and whether progress genuinely requires a larger scale of resources or capability.
The possible outcomes should therefore be: Continue • Expand • Redirect • Conclude.

The ability to redirect or conclude programmes is important. An exploratory investigation demonstrating that a proposed approach is unlikely to succeed may itself have generated valuable knowledge. A healthy scientific system should therefore reward learning, not merely expansion.
Increasing community engagement with increasing scale

INPA's involvement should also be proportional to the national significance of the programme. At Tier I, initiatives will largely remain investigator- and institution-driven. At Tier II, INPA/NNPI can increasingly facilitate connections among groups and help build collaborations. At Tier III, a substantial community-planning process and broader NNPI engagement become appropriate. At Tier IV, broad national consultation and structured interaction with institutions, funding agencies and government become essential.
People must progress with programmes
The tiered pathway should not describe only the growth of projects. It should also create a pathway for the growth of scientists.
As programmes grow, researchers should gain responsibility for work they can eventually direct.
Projects can build shared expertise and, where justified, capabilities or infrastructure for the wider community.
This parallel development of science, people and capability is one of the central purposes of NNPI.

sections.title: 3.4 Programme Evaluation and the Role of Agencies

blocks.text: Every NNPI programme should have a clear route to independent scientific evaluation. The proposal should identify the body responsible for evaluating it, the expertise required for that evaluation, and the decisions the review is expected to inform. A small exploratory study may require a short review by specialists. A national facility proposal warrants a fuller assessment of the science case, technical feasibility, costs and long-term institutional commitments.
Who should evaluate a programme?

text.text: INPA

should convene the scientific community to identify priorities, bring potential partners together and help develop the initial science case. Its endorsement can explain why a programme matters to Indian nuclear physics and where it fits within the national portfolio.
The
lead institution or consortium

should take responsibility for the proposal, including its technical plan, staffing, costs and commitments from partners. Once the programme begins, it should report progress and act on review findings.
The
agency with the relevant mandate

should arrange independent peer review and decide whether to fund or authorise the work within its remit. The appropriate agency should be identified for each programme. For proposals involving several agencies, the partners should agree early on which body will lead the evaluation, what each agency is being asked to support, and how subsequent reviews will be coordinated.

blocks.text: What should reviewers assess?

At the proposal stage, reviewers should ask whether the scientific question is important, whether the proposed approach can answer it, and whether the team has the capability and resources to carry out the work. For larger programmes, the panel should bring together scientific and technical expertise and examine alternatives, including better use or upgrading of existing facilities. It should also assess who will use the capability, how users will gain access, and who will sustain it after the initial funding period.

Once a programme is underway, the review should ask what has been learned and what that evidence justifies. A prototype may have done its job if it reveals a technical limitation early. A collaborative programme may merit expansion if it produces strong science and demonstrates demand beyond its founding institutions. For a national capability, user access, reliability, scientific output and the development of new expertise all matter.

text.text: Each review should end with a clear recommendation to
continue, expand, redirect or conclude

the programme. The reviewing body should record the reasons, the lead institution should identify the actions it will take, and the responsible agency should decide on any change in funding or commitments.

blocks.text: NNPI should begin with a small number of scientific priorities for which institutions are willing to take responsibility and a credible first step can be defined. An initial programme might bring together researchers around a shared scientific question, test a detector prototype or open an existing capability to a wider group of users. Each should have a clear scientific purpose, a lead institution and a first milestone against which progress can be assessed.
Choosing the first programmes

INPA should invite researchers at universities, national laboratories and other institutions to identify scientific questions that would benefit from a coordinated effort. The emerging NNPI landscape can help match these ideas with research groups, facilities and expertise across the country. The first round should favour ideas with a compelling scientific case, committed partners and a realistic starting point. It should also give early-career researchers opportunities to propose work and take responsibility for carrying it out.
Turning priorities into proposals

For each selected priority, a lead institution or consortium should prepare a short programme brief. It should state the scientific objective, the first milestone, the responsibilities of each partner, and the facility access, staff time and funding needed to begin. Where a proposal requires external support, the lead institution should identify the agency with the relevant mandate and seek evaluation through the process described in Section 3.4. Work that can begin with existing resources can proceed once the participating institutions agree on their commitments.
Learning from the first round

After the first milestones, INPA should bring the participating teams together to discuss what helped the programmes get started and where they encountered obstacles. Several teams may, for example, need access to the same facility, support from the same instrumentation specialists or a better way to involve researchers from smaller institutions. Identifying these shared needs can shape the next round of priorities and reveal where a broader national capability is warranted.
The first round will have served its purpose if it advances worthwhile science and shows how institutions can turn a shared priority into work they are prepared to own and sustain.
Comments on the draft and suggestions for the first NNPI programmes are welcome. The following questions may help guide responses.

items: Which scientific questions should NNPI take up first, and what could a first project achieve?
Which institutions or research groups could take the lead, and what capabilities could partners contribute?
What facility access, staff time or funding would be needed to get started, and which agency should review a proposal that needs external support?
Where could early-career researchers take responsibility for a first project, prototype or training programme?
What should INPA and participating institutions look for when deciding whether to continue, expand, redirect or conclude the first programmes?
